query:
The energy charge of the cell is:
A. the difference between the charge on the outside and inside of a cell.
B. generated by the sodium-potassium ATPase.
C. the overall rate of energy use by the cell.
D. the extent to which the total adenine nucleotide pool is phosphorylated.

conflictual_element.title: Physiology, Nerve -- Mechanism
conflictual_element.text: Nerve impulses get conveyed and transmitted via action potentials, which are brief changes in membrane potential. Neurons have a resting membrane potential around -60mV; this is due to a layer of negatively charged ions on the inner cell membrane of the neuron and a layer of positively charged ions on the outer cell membrane. This separation of charge results in electrical potential, which at rest (not during an action potential) is 60 mV more negative in the cell interior. This potential is generated from the movement of sodium, potassium, and chloride ions into and out of the cell down their concentration and electrical gradients, with the Na-K pump, actively pumping sodium and potassium against their concentration gradient to prevent concentration equilibrium. The potassium concentration inside a neuron is high, and sodium concentration is relatively low, so potassium ions are driven out of the cell by their concentration gradient while sodium ions are driven inside the cell - this is balanced by the electrical gradient as well, with the negatively charged cell interior pulling positively charged ions inside. The neuron cell membrane is most permeable to potassium due to a large - amount of potassium channels, so the resting cell membrane of the neuron is most affected by relative potassium concentrations. [10] [11] [12]

conflictual_element.title: Physiology, Resting Potential -- Mechanism
conflictual_element.text: Na+ and K+ do not reach electrochemical equilibrium. Even though a small amount of Na+ ions can enter the cell and K+ ions can leave the cell via K+ leak channels, the Na+/K+ pump constantly uses energy to maintain these gradients. [7] This pump plays a large role in maintaining the ionic concentration gradient by exchanging 3 Na+ ions from inside the cell, for every 2 K+ ions brought into the cell. We must stress that while this pump does not make a significant contribution to the charge of the membrane potential, it is crucial in maintaining the ionic gradients of Na+ and K+ across the membrane. What generates the resting membrane potential is the K+ that leaks from the inside of the cell to the outside via leak K+ channels and generates a negative charge in the inside of the membrane vs the outside. At rest, the membrane is impermeable to Na+, as all of the Na+ channels are closed.

conflictual_element.text: The Na + /K + pump uses ATP to transport 3 Na + ions extracellularly and 2 K + ions intracellularly. This process causes the intracellular pooling of K and the extracellular pooling of Na. [6] According to natural diffusion, molecules always move from a region of high concentration to a region of low concentration (down their concentration gradient). The cell membrane contains many K "leak" channels, which allow the high intracellular K to flow down its chemical gradient and exit the cell. These channels are always open, so they are always "leaking" potassium out of the cell. Potassium ions have a positive charge. When K ions move from inside to the outside of the cell via its chemical gradient, these positive ions deposit on the outside of the membrane, creating transmembrane electrical potential with a positive charge outside of the membrane and negative charge on the inside of the membrane; this transmembrane potential creates the electrical gradient of the cell membrane in which anything with a positive charge attempt to flow down its electrical gradient and move intracellularly. In theory, ions stop moving across the cell membrane when the ion's chemical gradient equals its electrical gradient; at this point, the cell membrane is at its resting membrane potential. The cell membrane has varying permeability to Na + , K + , and Cl - , with K + being the most permeable in the resting state; thus, K + has the greatest influence on the cell's resting membrane potential. [7]

conflictual_element.title: Physiology, Phosphate -- Function
conflictual_element.text: Cellular functions : In the cells, phosphate is an important component of the lipid bilayer of cell membranes, DNA, RNA, and proteins. It is responsible for several enzymatic reactions within the cells, e.g., glycolysis and ammoniagenesis. conflictual_element.title: Parametric probe 1
conflictual_element.text:
D. the extent to which the total adenine nucleotide pool is phosphorylated.

Explanation: The energy charge of a cell refers to the ratio of the number of high-energy phosphate groups (such as ATP, ADP, and AMP) to the total number of adenine nucleotides in the cell's adenine nucleotide pool. This measure reflects the cell's ability to rapidly generate ATP through cellular respiration and glycolysis, indicating its current energy state and metabolic activity. It does not directly relate to the charge across the cell membrane, nor is it directly related to the sodium-potassium ATPase or the overall rate of energy use.

conflictual_element.title: Parametric probe 7
conflictual_element.text:
D. the extent to which the total adenine nucleotide pool is phosphorylated.

The energy charge (EC) of a cell is defined as the ratio of the total phosphorylated adenine nucleotides to the total adenine nucleotides in the cell's adenine nucleotide pool, typically referring to ADP (adenosine diphosphate) and ATP (adenosine triphosphate). This measure reflects the relative balance of high-energy phosphate bonds in cellular energy stores compared to the overall nucleotide content. 

Options A, B, and C describe different concepts related to cell function but do not accurately define the energy charge:

- Option A refers to membrane potential, which is a voltage difference across the cell membrane, not the energy charge.
- Option B describes the sodium-potassium ATPase, which is an ion pump involved in maintaining cellular ionic gradients but does not generate the energy charge itself.
- Option C refers to the rate of cellular energy usage, which is not a direct measure of the energy charge. The energy charge considers the state of energy storage rather than its immediate consumption.

conflictual_element.text: Choose the ONE best answer. .1. Which one of the following statements concerning the titration curve for a nonpolar amino acid is correct? The letters A through D designate certain regions on the curve below. A. Point A represents the region where the amino acid is deprotonated. B. Point B represents a region of minimal buffering. C. non_conflictual_elements.title: InternalMed_Harrison
non_conflictual_elements.text: Primitive Reflexes With disease of the frontal lobe pathways, several primitive reflexes not normally present in the adult may appear. The suck response is elicited by lightly touching with a tongue blade the center of the lips, and the root response the corner of the lips; the patient will move the lips to suck or root in the direction of the stimulus. The grasp reflex is elicited by touching the palm between the thumb and index finger with the examiner’s fingers; a positive response is a forced grasp of the examiner’s hand. In many instances, stroking the back of the hand will lead to its release. The palmomental response is contraction of the mentalis muscle (chin) ipsilateral to a scratch stimulus diagonally applied to the palm. • The bare minimum: Ask whether the patient can feel light touch and the temperature of a cool object in each distal extremity. Check double simultaneous stimulation using light touch on the hands. Perform the Romberg maneuver.

non_conflictual_elements.title: Anatomy_Gray
non_conflictual_elements.text: The hand as a mechanical tool One of the major functions of the hand is to grip and manipulate objects. Gripping objects generally involves flexing the fingers against the thumb. Depending on the type of grip, muscles in the hand act to: modify the actions of long tendons that emerge from the forearm and insert into the digits of the hand, and produce combinations of joint movements within each digit that cannot be generated by the long flexor and extensor tendons alone coming from the forearm. The hand as a sensory tool The hand is used to discriminate between objects on the basis of touch. The pads on the palmar aspect of the fingers contain a high density of somatic sensory receptors. Also, the sensory cortex of the brain devoted to interpreting information from the hand, particularly from the thumb, is disproportionately large relative to that for many other regions of skin.

non_conflictual_elements.text: The pilosebaceous unit, containing hair follicles, works to produce hair fibers and oils, participates in wound healing, and holds reserves of immune cells and pigment-producing cells. The isthmus and upper bulge region of a hair follicle contains a piloneural collar. The piloneural collar contains mechanoreceptors that transmit sensation through the hair follicle. Different hair follicle types are defined by their length, hair shaft thickness, and kinks. The types are called zigzag, auchene/awl, and guard. [13] [14] Piloneural collars can contain all three types of sensory neurons; A-beta, A-delta, or C fibers. A-beta fibers were previously discussed in conjunction with Merkel cells touch domes. A-delta cells can be hair follicle specific, sometimes called D-Hair units, and are the most sensitive hair follicle mechanoreceptor. Some A-delta fibers are circumferentially wrapped around the base of hair follicles, while others have longitudinal lanceolate endings. These D-Hair units are associated with the awl/auchene and zigzag hair follicles and detect the movements of the small sinuses and down hairs in mammals. It is still unknown how these cells affect touch perception. C fibers are associated with painful stimuli, pleasurable touches, and sensations such as tickling. C fibers are the most numerous and are activated by indentation that moves slowly across their field, called caressing touches. Which of the following is true about rectal bleeding?
A. A painful digital examination suggests an anal fissure
B. Bright red blood on the finger usually signifies a caecal lesion
C. Proctoscopy is of no value in the assessment of rectal bleeding
D. Rectal cancer is the commonest cause of rectal bleeding

conflictual_element.title: Rectal Bleeding -- History and Physical -- Physical Examination
conflictual_element.text: Digital rectal examination is crucial for evaluating rectal bleeding and must be performed thoroughly. Anorectal polyps, malignant neoplasms, thrombosed internal hemorrhoids, radiation proctitis, solitary rectal ulcer syndrome, and complex fistula in ano can be readily diagnosed with a rectal examination. The examining digit should be checked for blood color, association with feces, and the presence of mucus or pus. Rectal examination should not be performed in patients with acute anal fissure, as this can be extremely painful and can induce vasovagal syncope. Rectal examination is also contraindicated in patients who are severely immunocompromised or on chemotherapy. Please see StatPearls' companion resource, Rectal Exam, for further information. Proctoscopy or anoscopy is generally performed after a rectal examination to diagnose anorectal conditions such as hemorrhoids, polyps, and malignant lesions. Videoproctoscopy is an office procedure that provides high-definition images of the anal canal and lower rectum and can be used to diagnose and follow up on various anorectal conditions that cause rectal bleeding. [29]

conflictual_element.title: Parametric probe 6
conflictual_element.text:
A. A painful digital examination suggests an anal fissure.
Explanation: 
A. A painful digital examination suggests an anal fissure - This statement is true. An anal fissure, a tear in the lining of the anus, typically causes severe pain during and after a digital (finger) examination. The presence of pain during this test is often diagnostic for an anal fissure.

B. Bright red blood on the finger usually signifies a caecal lesion - This statement is false. Bright red blood on the finger during a digital examination is more indicative of hemorrhoids or minor rectal bleeding due to irritation rather than a caecal lesion (which refers to a condition affecting the lower part of the small intestine). Caecal lesions would generally not cause bright red blood visible on a finger.

C. Proctoscopy is of no value in the assessment of rectal bleeding - This statement is false. Proctoscopy, which involves examining the rectum with a special instrument called a proctoscope, can be very valuable in assessing rectal bleeding. It allows direct visualization of the rectal lining and helps identify sources of bleeding, including hemorrhoids, polyps, or early signs of colorectal cancer.

D. Rectal cancer is the commonest cause of rectal bleeding -

non_conflictual_elements.title: Rectal Bleeding -- History and Physical -- History
non_conflictual_elements.text: Rectal bleeding associated with anal or perianal pain is often suggestive of an anorectal cause. The most common differential is an anal fissure, which is usually associated with a history of constipation, straining, and passage of hard stools. Etiologies like perianal Crohn disease, tuberculosis, and sexually transmitted infections should be considered in patients with atypical or recurrent anal fissures. non_conflictual_elements.text: The second serious interaction with MAOIs occurs when an MAOI is combined with tyramine in the diet or with sympathomimetic substrates of MAO. An MAOI prevents the breakdown of tyramine in the gut, and this results in high serum levels that enhance peripheral noradrenergic effects, including raising blood pressure dramatically. Patients on an MAOI who ingest large amounts of dietary tyramine may experience malignant hypertension and subsequently a stroke or myocardial infarction. conflictual_element.title: Neuroanatomy, Prefrontal Cortex -- Introduction
conflictual_element.text: Why are we capable of doing things that are difficult, of making choices to go the hard route or the extra mile? Much of this ability can be attributed to the bulk of the frontal cortex in an area known as the prefrontal cortex (PFC). It is where we process moment-to-moment input from our surroundings, compare that input to past experiences, and then react to them. non_conflictual_elements.title: Hypoxic-Ischemic Encephalopathy -- Differential Diagnosis
non_conflictual_elements.text: Locked-in syndrome is a state in which self-awareness is likely to be present, along with preservation of the sleep-wake cycle. Typically, this results in persistent quadriplegia, although it does have the potential for prolonged survivability. Akinetic mutism, a condition where damage to the frontal lobe of the brain results in a lack of movement or speech initiation, is also a potential condition that may be the result of anoxic injury, among other causes. Dementia, particularly advanced dementia, should also be considered, especially with a known history. [18] A physical feature that may be present is post-hypoxic myoclonus. [4] [5] While this suggests a hypoxic insult likely from anoxic injury, consideration of status epilepticus or other seizure activity is warranted. Evaluation with continuous EEG is ideal if available. A bispectral index can also be utilized; however, it is more limited in its ability to monitor multiple regions of the brain. In addition to seizure disorders, the Lance-Adams syndrome also correlates with myoclonus but has a favorable neurologic outcome. Neurology consultation may help to distinguish post-hypoxic myoclonus from Lance-Adams syndrome.

non_conflictual_elements.text:
D. Visual perception.

The frontal lobe of the brain's cortex is primarily associated with visual perception, along with other functions such as planning, decision-making, and voluntary movement. Therefore, the most accurate answer among the given options is D. Visual perception.

non_conflictual_elements.title: Parametric probe 2
non_conflictual_elements.text:
C. Understanding others' speech.

The frontal lobe of the brain, particularly its inferior frontal gyrus (Broca's area) and superior frontal gyrus (premotor cortex), plays a crucial role in understanding language, including the comprehension of spoken words and sentences. This function is essential for processing and interpreting speech from others. 

The other options describe functions that are primarily associated with other brain regions:
- The sleep/wake cycle is regulated by various parts of the brain, including the hypothalamus and the suprachiasmatic nucleus.
- Drawing shapes typically involves motor skills controlled by the primary motor cortex and requires fine motor control, not language processing.
- Visual perception is mainly handled by the occipital lobe and related structures. While some aspects of visual information processing can involve the frontal lobe, this function is more complex and broader than just visual perception itself.

non_conflictual_elements.title: Parametric probe 3
non_conflictual_elements.text:
D. Visual perception.
The frontal lobe, located at the front of each cerebral hemisphere, plays a crucial role in various cognitive functions. Among these, visual perception is one of its primary responsibilities. Damage or dysfunction in this area can lead to difficulties with recognizing objects, faces, and other visual stimuli, as well as issues with spatial awareness and navigation. While other functions such as motor control and decision-making are also associated with the frontal lobe, visual processing specifically falls under its domain.

non_conflictual_elements.title: Parametric probe 6
non_conflictual_elements.text:
D. Visual perception.

The frontal lobe primarily controls functions related to higher-order cognitive processes, motor planning, and decision-making, rather than specific sensory or motor skills like drawing shapes or visual perception. It does not directly manage the sleep-wake cycle (which is regulated by the hypothalamus and other areas) or the comprehension of spoken language (which involves parts of the temporal lobe and Wernicke's area). Therefore, while the frontal lobe plays a role in many aspects of cognition and behavior, its main responsibilities do not include the ability to draw shapes or understanding others' speech. The primary function of the frontal lobe with respect to visual processing is less direct; it influences motor coordination involved in eye movements and gaze direction, but visual perception itself is mainly handled by the occipital lobe.

conflictual_element.title: Anatomy_Gray
conflictual_element.text: The small carpal bones of the wrist are arranged in two rows, a proximal and a distal row, each consisting of four bones (Fig. 7.94). From lateral to medial and when viewed from anteriorly, the proximal row of bones consists of: the boat-shaped scaphoid, the lunate, which has a crescent shape, the three-sided triquetrum bone, and the pea-shaped pisiform (Fig. 7.94). The pisiform is a sesamoid bone in the tendon of the flexor carpi ulnaris and articulates with the anterior surface of the triquetrum. The scaphoid has a prominent tubercle on its lateral palmar surface that is directed anteriorly. From lateral to medial and when viewed from anteriorly, the distal row of carpal bones consists of: the irregular four-sided trapezium bone, the four-sided trapezoid, the capitate, which has a head, and the hamate, which has a hook (Fig. 7.94). The trapezium articulates with the metacarpal bone of the thumb and has a distinct tubercle on its palmar surface that projects anteriorly.

conflictual_element.title: Upper Limb Amputation -- Anatomy and Physiology -- Wrist

conflictual_element.title: Anatomy, Shoulder and Upper Limb, Hand Carpal Bones -- Introduction
conflictual_element.text: The carpal bones are bones of the wrist that connect the distal aspects of the radial and ulnar bones of the forearm to the bases of the 5 metacarpal bones of the hand (see Image. Normal Posteroanterior Radiograph of the Wrist Joint). Eight carpal bones divide into 2 rows: proximal and distal rows (see Image. Normal Lateral Radiograph of the Wrist Joint). Left Hand, Anterior View).

2. Lunate

4. Pisiform

It's important to note that the term "proximal phalynx" is not related to the carpal bones; it refers to the proximal phalanx, which is one of the bones in the fingers. conflictual_element.text: The anatomy of the wrist joint is complex, composed of numerous bones, ligaments, tendons, and cartilaginous structures. The major ligament of the wrist is the triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC), which keeps the wrist joint stable while pronating and supinating the arm. Which one of the following statements is true with regard to intravenous drug administration?
A. IV administration of a drug will delay its action.
B. IV administration carries low risk of bacteraemia.
C. IV administration allows titration of a drug with its desired effect.
D. An intravenous cannula should never be used for both drug and fluid administration.

conflictual_element.title: Parametric probe 1
conflictual_element.text:
C. IV administration allows titration of a drug with its desired effect.

Explanation: Intravenous (IV) drug administration allows for precise control over the dosage and timing of medication, enabling healthcare providers to achieve the desired therapeutic effect while minimizing adverse reactions. This level of control is crucial for managing dosing in various clinical scenarios, such as cancer chemotherapy, where precise control is essential to maximize efficacy and minimize toxicity. 

Option A is false because IV administration can actually speed up drug delivery compared to oral or other routes. Option B is not entirely accurate as there is always some risk of bacteraemia when using any invasive route of administration. Option D is also incorrect as it oversimplifies the practice of using IV cannulas; they can be used for both drugs and fluids under appropriate conditions, though this practice must be managed carefully to prevent complications.

conflictual_element.title: Parametric probe 3
conflictual_element.text:
C. IV administration allows titration of a drug with its desired effect.

Explanation:
- A. IV administration typically does not delay the action of drugs; it can actually enhance absorption, making this statement false.
- B. IV administration indeed carries a lower risk of bacteremia compared to other routes due to the sterile environment, so this is a true statement.
- C. This is correct because IV administration allows for precise control over drug dosing and monitoring of effects, facilitating titration to achieve the desired therapeutic outcome.
- D. Using an IV cannula for both drug and fluid administration is generally safe and recommended when necessary, as long as proper aseptic technique is followed. Therefore, this statement is false.

non_conflictual_elements.text: The route of administration (ROA) and the drug dose can significantly impact both the rate and extent of bioavailability. The dose of a drug is indirectly proportional to its bioavailability (Equation 5). A drug with relatively low bioavailability requires a larger dose to reach the minimum effective concentration threshold. The various routes of administration each contain a unique capability to facilitate a certain plasma drug concentration for a certain length of time. In many cases, altering the route of administration calls for an alteration of the dosage. For example, an oral drug requires passage through the gastrointestinal (GI) system, subjecting it to intestinal absorption and hepatic first-pass metabolism. conflictual_element.title: Physiology, Adenosine Triphosphate -- Mechanism -- Cellular Respiration
conflictual_element.text: Cellular respiration is the process of catabolizing glucose into acetyl-CoA, producing high-energy electron carriers that are oxidized during oxidative phosphorylation, thereby generating ATP. During glycolysis, the first step in cellular respiration, 1 glucose molecule is converted into 2 pyruvate molecules. During this process, 2 ATP are produced through substrate phosphorylation by the enzymes PFK1 and pyruvate kinase. There is also the production of 2 reduced NADH electron carrier molecules. The pyruvate molecules are then oxidized by the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex, yielding acetyl-CoA. The acetyl-CoA molecule is then fully oxidized to yield carbon dioxide and reduced electron carriers in the citric acid cycle. Upon completing the citric acid cycle, the total yield is 2 molecules of carbon dioxide, 1 equivalent of ATP, 3 molecules of NADH, and 1 molecule of FADH2. These high-energy electron carriers then transfer electrons to the electron transport chain, in which hydrogen ions (protons) are transported against their electrochemical gradient into the inner mitochondrial membrane space from the mitochondrial matrix. ATP molecules are then synthesized as protons move down the electrochemical gradient through ATP synthase. [9] The amount of ATP produced depends on which electron carrier donates protons. One NADH molecule produces 2 and a half ATP, whereas 1 FADH2 molecule produces 1 and a half ATP molecules. [17]

non_conflictual_elements.text:
A. A low blood pressure (<90mmHg systolic) and a tachycardia (>100/min) are worrying features

Explanation:
Haematemesis (vomiting of blood) typically indicates significant upper gastrointestinal bleeding. The presence of hypotension (low blood pressure, <90 mmHg systolic) and tachycardia (heart rate >100 beats per minute) are indeed concerning signs that suggest severe blood loss. This combination can be life-threatening and requires immediate attention.

B. A pulse rate of 80/min in a patient taking Bisoprolol is reassuring - This statement is false. Bisoprolol is a beta-blocker that may mask symptoms of hypotension or heart failure. A pulse rate of 80/min could be normal for someone on this medication, but it does not guarantee safety.

C. Abdominal pain is always present - This statement is false. While abdominal pain is often associated with upper gastrointestinal bleeding, it is not always present. Other presentations may include nausea, vomiting, or altered mental status due to anemia.

D. An alcohol history is not essential - This statement is false. Alcohol consumption can significantly increase the risk of upper gastrointestinal bleeding

The carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) is indeed associated with rheumatoid arthritis, as inflammation from the condition can lead to thickening of the tendons in the wrist, narrowing the carpal tunnel, and compressing the median nerve. 

B is incorrect because CTS is primarily caused by compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel rather than compression of the ulnar nerve.
 
C is correct - CTS typically results in pain and tingling sensations in the thumb, index, and middle fingers, which are the "medial three and half digits."

D is inaccurate as paraesthesia (a feeling of tingling or numbness) in CTS tends to be more pronounced at night due to the position of the wrist during sleep, rather than being worse during the day. 

Therefore, the only accurate statement among the given options is A. It can be caused by rheumatoid arthritis.

Compression of the median nerve at the wrist (carpal tunnel syndrome) is the most common disorder affecting the median nerve and the most frequent nerve entrapment syndrome. The problem arises usually as a result of excessive use of the hands and occupational microtrauma. Infiltration of the transverse carpal ligament with amyloid (as occurs in multiple myeloma and amyloidosis) or thickening of connective tissue in rheumatoid arthritis, acromegaly, mucopolysaccharidosis, and hypothyroidism are less commonly identified causes. It is also common for the condition to make its appearance during pregnancy. In elderly individuals, the cause of the carpal tunnel syndrome is often not apparent. non_conflictual_elements.title: Rheumatic Manifestations of Metabolic Disease -- History and Physical -- Carpal tunnel syndrome
non_conflictual_elements.text: CTS involves median nerve compression, leading to neuropathy. Patients frequently experience numbness, tingling, and pain in areas innervated by the medial nerve, ie, the thumb and the second, third, and radial portion of the fourth finger. The symptoms vary in intensity but tend to worsen at night. Advanced disease can cause sensory loss and muscle deformation due to weakness. Several maneuvers are used to diagnose CTS. The carpal compression test is positive if paresthesia or pain is evident after applying pressure to the carpal tunnel for 30 seconds. The test has a sensitivity of 64% and a specificity of 83%. The Phalen test is positive when pain and paresthesia are present when the patient flexes and holds their hands together for 1 minute. This test has a sensitivity of 68% and a specificity of 73%. non_conflictual_elements.text: Compression of the ulnar nerve is the second most common entrapment neuropathy after carpal tunnel syndrome. The most frequent site of compression is at the elbow where the nerve passes superficially in the ulnar groove. Symptoms usually begin with tingling in the ulnar distribution, including the fourth and fifth digits of the hand (Fig. 463e-3B). Sensory symptoms may be worsened by elbow flexion due to increased pressure on the nerve, hence the tendency of patients to complain of increasing paresthesias at night when the arm is flexed at the elbow during sleep. Motor dysfunction can be disabling and involves most of the intrinsic hand muscles, limiting dexterity and strength of grasp and pinch. Etiologies of ulnar entrapment include trauma to the nerve (hitting the “funny bone”), malpositioning during anesthesia for surgical procedures, and chronic arthritis of the elbow. non_conflictual_elements.title: Anatomy_Gray
non_conflictual_elements.text: In the clinic Carpal tunnel syndrome is an entrapment syndrome caused by pressure on the median nerve within the carpal tunnel. The etiology of this condition is often obscure, though in some instances the nerve injury may be a direct effect of increased pressure on the median nerve caused by overuse, swelling of the tendons and tendon sheaths (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis), and cysts arising from the carpal joints. Increased pressure in the carpal tunnel is thought to cause venous congestion that produces nerve edema and anoxic damage to the capillary endothelium of the median nerve itself. Patients typically report pain and pins-and-needles sensations in the distribution of the median nerve. Weakness and loss of muscle bulk of the thenar muscles may also occur. Gently tapping over the median nerve (in the region of the flexor retinaculum) readily produces these symptoms (Tinel’s sign).

non_conflictual_elements.text:
A. It can be caused by rheumatoid arthritis

Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) is typically caused by compression of the median nerve as it passes through the carpal tunnel in the wrist. While CTS can occur due to various conditions, including repetitive hand use or trauma, rheumatoid arthritis can contribute to its development by causing inflammation and swelling that narrows the tunnel and compresses the median nerve. The other options contain inaccuracies:

- B is incorrect because the ulnar nerve, not the ulna nerve, is involved.
- C is incorrect; the symptoms usually affect the radial three and a half digits (thumb, index, middle, ring fingers), not the medial ones.
- D is incorrect; paraesthesia (tingling or numbness) in CTS tends to be worse at night rather than during the day.

non_conflictual_elements.title: Parametric probe 4
non_conflictual_elements.text:
A. It can be caused by rheumatoid arthritis.
C. It causes pain and tingling in the medial three and half digits.

Explanation:
A. Carpal tunnel syndrome (CTS) can indeed be associated with rheumatoid arthritis due to the inflammatory nature of the condition which can lead to swelling in the wrist and hand, potentially compressing the median nerve.
C. This statement is accurate. CTS typically affects the thumb, index, middle, and part of the ring fingers, often referred to as the "median nerve territory." The symptoms you describe correspond to these areas.
D. The severity of paraesthesia (a sensation of tingling or numbness) can vary throughout the day; however, it is more commonly reported at night when lying down, not necessarily worse during the day. Therefore, this option is not entirely correct. 

Note: B is incorrect because the ulnar nerve, not the ulna nerve, is compressed in carpal tunnel syndrome, leading to symptoms such as pain and numbness in the fourth and fifth digits (the "ulnar nerve territory").

non_conflictual_elements.title: Parametric probe 5
non_conflictual_elements.text:
A. It can be caused by rheumatoid arthritis.
C. It causes pain and tingling in the medial three and half digits.

Explanation:
- Option A (It can be caused by rheumatoid arthritis) is correct. Rheumatoid arthritis can lead to inflammation and swelling of the tissues around the carpal tunnel, which can compress the median nerve and cause carpal tunnel syndrome.
- Option C (It causes pain and tingling in the medial three and half digits) is also correct. The symptoms of carpal tunnel syndrome typically involve numbness, tingling, or pain in the thumb, index, and middle fingers, collectively known as the "median nerve distribution."
- Option B (It is caused by compression of the ulnar nerve) is incorrect. Carpal tunnel syndrome is specifically caused by compression of the median nerve.
- Option D (Paraesthesia is worse during the day) is incorrect. While the symptoms can be more pronounced at night due to sleeping positions, paraesthesia (numbness and tingling) is not typically worse during the day compared to nighttime.

B. the entire DNA sequence of an organism.

The genome refers to the complete set of DNA sequences (both coding and non-coding regions) within an organism's cells, including all of its genes and regulatory elements. This includes the entire DNA sequence present in the nucleus and sometimes in mitochondria or chloroplasts. It does not specifically refer to the number of chromosomes (which is a characteristic of karyotypes), nor does it encompass just the protein-coding genes (which would be a subset of the genome). The genome is comprehensive, containing all genetic information necessary for an organism's development, functioning, and reproduction.

conflictual_element.text: Peptide bonds join together the 20 amino acids found in proteins. The linear sequence of the linked amino acids contains the information necessary to generate a protein molecule with a specific 3-dimensional shape. The sequence of amino acids in a protein is referred to as the primary structure of the protein. The sequence of nucleotides in a protein-coding region of the DNA specifies the amino acid sequence of a polypeptide. The polypeptide backbone of proteins does not form a random 3-dimensional structure; instead, the regular arrangements of amino acids are located near each other in the linear sequence. These arrangements are commonly termed the secondary structure of the polypeptide or protein. The α-helix and β-sheet are examples of secondary structures normally found in proteins. The primary structure of a polypeptide chain determines the final tertiary structure, which refers to the folding of domains and the final arrangement of domains in the protein.

non_conflictual_elements.title: Genetics, Nondisjunction -- Cellular
non_conflictual_elements.text: The genome is encoded by the chemical sequence of DNA nucleotides within our cells. In periods of cell growth, histone proteins around DNA are acetylated causing less interaction between the DNA and histone protein. This opened DNA is called euchromatin and allows transcriptional enzymes access to the DNA. Before periods of cell division, the histone proteins are deacetylated allowing for the formation of a condensed form of DNA called heterochromatin. Somatic human cells contain 23 paired chromosomes or 46 total chromosomes. Forty-six is considered the “diploid” number (2n), while 23 is considered the “haploid” number (1n) or half the diploid number. “Aneuploidy” refers to the presence of an abnormal number of chromosomes. Monosomy (n-1) is a form of aneuploidy characterized by missing a single chromosome resulting in 45 total chromosomes. Trisomy (n+1) is another form of aneuploidy that has an extra chromosome resulting in 47 total chromosomes. Each type of aneuploidy can be attributed to nondisjunction during mitosis or meiosis. A whole-genome duplication can occur quite simply: all that is required is one round of genome replication in a germ-line cell lineage without a corresponding cell division. non_conflictual_elements.text: One might have predicted that the information present in genomes would be arranged in an orderly fashion, resembling a dictionary or a telephone directory. But it turns out that the genomes of most multicellular organisms are surprisingly disorderly, reflecting their chaotic evolutionary histories. The genes in these organisms largely consist of a long string of alternating short exons and long introns, as discussed in Chapter 4 (see Figure 4–15D). conflictual_element.text:
A. via protein transporters called GLUT4.

Glucose enters muscle cells primarily through glucose transporter 4 (GLUT4) protein transporters, which are activated by insulin to facilitate increased glucose uptake during periods of high blood sugar levels or insulin stimulation. While insulin is necessary for the translocation of GLUT4 from intracellular storage vesicles to the cell membrane, GLUT4 itself is not directly activated by insulin but rather responds to its presence. Hexokinase and monocarboxylate transporters do play roles in glucose metabolism within cells, but they are not primary glucose entry mechanisms into muscle cells.

conflictual_element.title: Physiology, Glucose Transporter Type 4 -- Cellular Level
conflictual_element.text: GLUT4 moves between intracellular compartments and the plasma membrane. The transporter resides within an intracellular tubulovesicular network connected to the endosomal and trans-Golgi network systems and changes location in response to stimulation. In the absence of insulin or exercise, 90% of GLUT4 remains intracellular. In the presence of insulin or exercise, GLUT4 storage vesicles undergo exocytosis to the plasma membrane, including the sarcolemma and T tubules of skeletal muscle cells, where the transporter facilitates glucose uptake. The resulting increase in GLUT4 molecules at the cell surface increases the maximal rate of glucose transport into cells. After insulin stimulation ceases, GLUT4 undergoes clathrin-mediated endocytosis through vesicles budding from the plasma membrane. Following internalization, GLUT4 enters early endosomes and is subsequently sorted into intracellular storage vesicles. [2] [3]

conflictual_element.title: Biochemistry, Telomere And Telomerase -- Mechanism
conflictual_element.text: DNA replication is facilitated by DNA polymerase. This enzyme can only synthesize DNA in the 5' to 3' direction. DNA replication begins with an RNA primer, which is synthesized by primase. The RNA primer allows the DNA to locate the area of the chromosome where replication begins. The RNA primer anneals to the template DNA to provide a free 3'-OH group where new nucleotides are added. During the synthesis of the leading strand, which runs from the 5' to 3' direction, only 1 primer is needed for synthesis at this location to be continuous. This is due to the addition of new nucleotides in the direction of the replication fork. [18] Simultaneously, the synthesis of the DNA strand occurs in a lagging fashion in the 3' to 5' direction. Multiple RNA primers are necessary for the lagging strand, which is then replaced by DNA nucleotides via DNA polymerase, elongated, and ligated to create the new DNA strand. [19] The challenge arises at the 5' end of the lagging strand, where a stretch of DNA the size of the RNA primer is lost. This "end replication problem" occurs when the final RNA primer is removed after complete replication. [20] DNA polymerase cannot synthesize the end of the lagging strand due to the lack of a 3'-OH group after removing the RNA primer. Thus, due to the inherent properties of DNA polymerase, after each S phase of cell division, telomeres shorten 50-150 base pairs. [21] [22]

The replication process is highly accurate, due to the proofreading ability of DNA polymerase. [12]

conflictual_element.text: D. Reverse transcriptases As seen with telomerase, reverse transcriptases are RNA-directed DNA pols. A reverse transcriptase is involved in the replication of retroviruses, such as human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). These viruses carry their genome in the form of ssRNA molecules. Following infection of a host cell, the viral enzyme reverse transcriptase uses the viral RNA as a template for the 5′→3′ synthesis of viral DNA, which then becomes integrated into host chromosomes. Reverse transcriptase activity is also seen with transposons, DNA elements that can move about the genome (see p. 477). In eukaryotes, most transposons are transcribed to RNA, the RNA is used as a template for DNA synthesis by a reverse transcriptase encoded by the transposon, and the DNA is randomly inserted into the genome. [Note: Transposons that involve an RNA intermediate are called retrotransposons or retroposons.] E. DNA replication inhibition by nucleoside analogs

conflictual_element.title: Biochemistry, Replication and Transcription -- Molecular Level -- Transcription
conflictual_element.text: RNA is synthesized from the DNA template by a process known as transcription. This requires the action of enzymes called RNA polymerases to generate a single-stranded RNA from one of the parent DNA strands. RNA synthesis requires RNA polymerase I for ribosomal RNA, RNA polymerase II for mRNA and microRNA, and RNA polymerase III for tRNA and other small RNAs. Transcription is not as accurate as replication and produces more errors. conflictual_element.text: Figure 8–31 The synthesis of cDNA. Total mRNA is extracted from a particular tissue, and the enzyme reverse transcriptase (see Figure 5–62) is used to produce DNA copies (cDNA) of the mRNA molecules. A short oligonucleotide complementary to the poly-A tail at the 3ʹ end of the mRNA (discussed in Chapter 6) is first hybridized to the RNA to act as a primer for the reverse transcriptase, which then copies the RNA into a complementary DNA chain, thereby forming a DNA–RNA hybrid helix. Treating the DNA–RNA hybrid with a specialized nuclease (RNAse H) that attacks only the RNA produces nicks and gaps in the RNA strand. conflictual_element.title: Variance -- Definition/Introduction
conflictual_element.text: Although the arithmetic mean of a set of numbers provides information about the center of that set, researchers need information about how the numbers are spread around that center to interpret the data correctly. [1] The variance provides a quantitative measure of how closely the data set is spread around its center. [2] A variance of smaller magnitude (closer to zero) implies that the set of numbers is quite tightly clustered around the center. A variance of larger magnitude (farther from zero) implies that at least some of the numbers in the data set are far away from the center. Importantly: (1) the variance can never be less than zero; (2) the variance is only equal to zero when all the numbers in the data set are equal, i.e., when the data set is composed of the same number repeated many times. In addition to being a summary statistic, the variance is often incorporated into other statistical outputs, such as confidence intervals. [3]

conflictual_element.text:
A. Genes are exchanged with other populations.

Explanation: The Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (HWE) is a principle that helps predict genetic variation in a population if certain conditions are met. For HWE to hold, the conditions listed should be true:

B. Population size must be large. - This ensures that genetic drift has little effect on allele frequencies.
C. Natural selection must not take place. - This prevents changes in allele frequencies due to differential survival and reproduction.

Option A, "Genes are exchanged with other populations," is incorrect because gene flow, or migration, actually disrupts the Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium. When there is gene flow, the allele frequencies change over time, making it impossible to achieve HWE. Therefore, gene flow is the condition that must be excluded for HWE to operate effectively.

conflictual_element.title: Variance -- Definition/Introduction
conflictual_element.text: Although the arithmetic mean of a set of numbers provides information about the center of that set, researchers need information about how the numbers are spread around that center to interpret the data correctly. [1] The variance provides a quantitative measure of how closely the data set is spread around its center. [2] A variance of smaller magnitude (closer to zero) implies that the set of numbers is quite tightly clustered around the center. A variance of larger magnitude (farther from zero) implies that at least some of the numbers in the data set are far away from the center. Importantly: (1) the variance can never be less than zero; (2) the variance is only equal to zero when all the numbers in the data set are equal, i.e., when the data set is composed of the same number repeated many times. In addition to being a summary statistic, the variance is often incorporated into other statistical outputs, such as confidence intervals. [3]

non_conflictual_elements.text: where P is the pressure, V is the volume, n is the number of moles of gas, R is the universal gas constant, and T is the absolute temperature. The modified version, the Van Der Waals equation, includes a for intermolecular forces and b to represent the volume of 1 mole of molecules. As such, this version better quantifies the behavior of real gases. The universal gas constant R is a number that satisfies the proportionalities of the pressure-volume-temperature relationship. R has different values and units that depend on the pressure, volume, moles, and temperature specifications. Various values are accepted for R through online databases, or dimensional analysis converts the observed units of pressure, volume, moles, and temperature to match a known R-value. As long as the units for pressure, volume, moles, and temperature are consistent, either approach is acceptable. The temperature value in the ideal gas law must be in absolute units, either Rankine (°R) or Kelvin (K), to prevent the right-hand side of the equation from being zero, which violates the pressure-volume-temperature relationship. The conversion from Fahrenheit (F) or Celsius (C) to absolute temperature units is a simple addition of a fixed value to the Fahrenheit (F) or the Celsius (C) temperature—°R=F+459.67 and K=C+273.15.

non_conflictual_elements.text: The acquisition of genetic mutations, particularly those that impact protein structure, function, or expression, is a prerequisite for natural selection, particularly if they significantly impact the organism’s phenotype. non_conflictual_elements.title: Parametric probe 1
non_conflictual_elements.text:

The concept of punctuated equilibrium, introduced by Niles Eldredge and Stephen Jay Gould, describes how evolutionary change occurs not through gradual transitions but rather through long periods of relative stability interrupted by rapid evolutionary changes. This theory explains that species do not usually evolve continuously over time but rather undergo major changes during short periods (punctuations) followed by long periods of little or no change (stasis). This contrasts with the more commonly accepted gradualism, which suggests that evolution happens slowly and steadily over long spans of time.

non_conflictual_elements.title: Parametric probe 6
non_conflictual_elements.text:
D. bursts of speciation followed by relatively unchanging lineages
The concept of punctuated equilibrium, proposed by Niles Eldredge and Stephen Jay Gould, suggests that evolutionary change is not gradual but occurs in fits and starts. During these periods of rapid evolution (bouts of speciation), species may undergo significant changes in their morphology, behavior, or genetics. However, after these bursts, there can be long periods of stasis where little to no evolutionary change occurs. This model challenges the traditional view of continuous, slow evolutionary change over geological time. 

To clarify why the other options are incorrect:
- Option A (oscillating ecological successional stages) describes a different biological process.
- Option B (ecological succession arrested by sudden environmental changes) is more accurately associated with catastrophic ecology rather than punctuated equilibrium.
- Option C (persistent predator-prey relationships in relatively stable environments) does not align with punctuated equilibrium, which focuses on evolutionary bursts rather than stable relationships.

query:
In Sweden, the red fox (Vulpes vulpes) severely limits populations of its prey, including hares. However, red fox populations are sometimes attacked by a fatal parasite, the mange mite. As mite population sizes increase at a given site, how are hare and fox populations most likely to respond at the same site? (Assume that hares have no major predators at this site other than foxes.)
A. Both fox and hare populations will decrease.
B. Both fox and hare populations will increase.
C. Fox populations will decrease and hare populations will increase.
D. Fox populations will increase and hare populations will decrease.

conflictual_element.title: Rabies -- History and Physical -- Rabies Exposure Risk Assessment
conflictual_element.text: Wild animals such as bats, raccoons, skunks, and foxes are the most common rabies carriers in the United States. However, other species, such as otters and coyotes, pose risks in specific locations ( CDC. Clinical Overview of Rabies ). Clinicians should ask whether the animal appeared unhealthy and obtain a description of its behavior. Exposure to healthy-appearing, normal-behaving rabbits, hares, and small rodents rarely constitutes a risk requiring PEP ( CDC. Clinical Overview of Rabies ). [9]

conflictual_element.title: Parametric probe 1
conflictual_element.text:
A. Both fox and hare populations will decrease.

Explanation:
In Sweden, the red fox (Vulpes vulpes) has been observed to significantly limit hare populations due to predation. When the red fox population is severely reduced by the mange mite parasite, it would allow the hare population to grow unchecked as there are fewer foxes to control their numbers.

With fewer foxes available to prey on hares, the hare population is likely to increase. However, with an abundance of hares, the red fox population may not be able to recover from the mange mite infection. The mange mite itself can cause severe skin problems for foxes, leading to higher mortality rates among the fox population.

Thus, both fox and hare populations are most likely to decrease at the same site when the fox population is severely impacted by the mange mite. This outcome results from a cascade effect in which fox predation pressure on hares is relieved, allowing hare populations to expand, but also causing a decline in the fox population due to the mange mite.

conflictual_element.title: Fox-Fordyce Disease (Apocrine Miliaria) -- Etiology
conflictual_element.text: The precise cause of Fox-Fordyce disease remains elusive. However, a critical factor in its etiopathogenesis appears to be the obstruction of the apocrine gland duct due to keratin accumulation in the follicular infundibulum. Several etiological hypotheses have been proposed for Fox-Fordyce disease. These include genetic factors, hormonal influences, laser hair reduction, and triggers that induce sweating. Familial inheritance: While Fox-Fordyce disease typically occurs sporadically, it is uncommon in sisters, monozygotic females, male twins, and daughter-father duos. [2] [3] [4] [5] Hormonal involvement: Fox-Fordyce disease commonly manifests in post-pubertal adolescent girls and women, with rarity in prepubertal and postmenopausal women, as well as men. Hormonal involvement is supported by premenstrual flare-ups and improvement during pregnancy, postmenopause, and with oral contraceptive pills. [6]

conflictual_element.title: Hymenoptera Envenomation -- Epidemiology
conflictual_element.text: Hymenoptera stings can happen in any age group, and the insects are not selective to a particular gender. Humans are most often stung by either accidental contact with a solitary worker (single sting from a single insect) or because they are near a disrupted nest (multiple stings from multiple insects). Occupations that may increase the risk of exposure to these stings include, but are not limited to, construction workers, landscapers, entomologists, beekeepers, and exterminators, among others. Vespidae (specifically hornets and yellow jackets) are likely the culprits in most situations due to their aggressive and territorial nature. Most sting reactions are self-limited, result in a small area of local inflammation, and resolve within a few days. Other local reactions may be larger, more painful, and last longer. These are less common (less than 10%) and termed large local reactions (LLRs) and may require medical intervention. Systemic reactions are far less common but can be fatal if they occur.

conflictual_element.text: The Vespidae family (wasps, yellow jackets, hornets) are known to be more aggressive than their Apidae relatives. They are found in all 50 states. Solitary wasps (mud wasps) usually make smaller nests in areas such as the sides of windows. Unlike the Apidae , the Vespidae family does not have a barbed stinger and hence, can sting multiple times.

non_conflictual_elements.text: The primary ecologic reservoir for the POW virus is rodents and small mammals. It has been most commonly isolated in mice, groundhogs, voles, and squirrels. non_conflictual_elements.title: InternalMed_Harrison
non_conflictual_elements.text: Human plague generally follows an outbreak in a host rodent population (epizootic). Mass deaths among the rodent primary hosts lead to a search by fleas for new hosts, with consequent incidental infection of other mammals. The precipitating cause for an epizootic may ultimately be related to climate or other environmental factors. The reservoir for Y. pestis causing enzootic plague in natural endemic foci between epizootics (i.e., when the organism may be difficult to detect in rodents or fleas) is a topic of ongoing research and may not be the same in all regions. The enzootic/epizootic pattern may be the result of complex dynamic interactions of host rodents that have different plague susceptibilities and different flea vectors; alternatively, an environmental reservoir may be important. In general, the enzootic areas for plague are lightly populated regions of Africa, Asia, and the Americas (Fig. 196-1).

conflictual_element.title: Parametric probe 2
conflictual_element.text:
D. I, II, and III

The cell nucleus indeed contains all three of these components:

1. **DNA (Deoxyribonucleic Acid)** - This is the primary genetic material that carries the instructions for the development, functioning, growth, and reproduction of all known living organisms. In the nucleus, it forms the chromosomes.

2. **Protein** - While proteins can be found in the cytoplasm and other cellular compartments, they play crucial roles within the nucleus as well. For example, histones, which are proteins, help package DNA into chromatin.

3. **RNA (Ribonucleic Acid)** - The nucleus produces RNA molecules, such as mRNA, which carry genetic information out of the nucleus to the ribosomes where protein synthesis occurs. Other types of RNA like tRNA and rRNA are also synthesized here.

Therefore, all three items listed (DNA, Protein, and RNA) are components of the cell nucleus. Thus, the correct answer is D. I, II, and III.

conflictual_element.title: Parametric probe 3
conflictual_element.text:
D. I, II, and III

1. **DNA (Deoxyribonucleic Acid)**: This is the primary genetic material that stores the hereditary information of an organism.
2. **Protein**: While not stored within the nucleus itself, proteins play crucial roles in many nuclear processes.
3. **RNA (Ribonucleic Acid)**: There are different types of RNA found in the nucleus, such as messenger RNA (mRNA), transfer RNA (tRNA), and ribosomal RNA (rRNA).

Thus, the correct answer is D: I, II, and III.

conflictual_element.title: Blood Product Safety -- Technique or Treatment
conflictual_element.text: An important aspect of the donation process is the donor-screening questionnaire. Donor recruitment represents a crucial frontline mechanism for ensuring blood safety. The highest rates of transfusion-transmitted infections are found among donors who receive monetary compensation, while the lowest rates of infection are observed among unpaid volunteer donors. [15] [16] "Replacement" and "family" donors are relied on in some countries, but these are not considered as safe as true altruistic, unpaid volunteers. A great reduction in the risk of transfusion-transmitted HIV, HCV, HBV, and syphilis infections has transpired with the initial donor screening questions and improved testing, including serology and nucleic acid amplification testing. [17] [18] According to the United States Food and Drug Administration, highly sensitive donor screening questionnaires designed to exclude high-risk donors for the transmission of infections exclude an estimated 90% of potentially infectious donors from blood donation. Donors who have incentives to donate (such as monetary gain or wanting to help a friend) may not be completely truthful during screening.

conflictual_element.title: Parametric probe 7
conflictual_element.text:
A. coefficient of relatedness
According to Hamilton's Rule, for an altruistic trait to evolve, the condition \( c < br \) must be satisfied, where:
- \( c \) represents the fitness cost to the donor (the individual performing the altruistic act),
- \( b \) represents the fitness benefit to the recipient (the individual benefiting from the altruistic act),
- \( r \) represents the coefficient of relatedness between the donor and the recipient.

The coefficient of relatedness \( r \) quantifies how closely genetically related the donor and the recipient are. If \( r \) is high, it means the recipient shares more genes with the donor than with a random individual, making the genetic benefits of the altruistic act more significant.

Thus, the correct answer is A. coefficient of relatedness.

conflictual_element.title: Parametric probe 6
conflictual_element.text:
A. coefficient of relatedness

Hamilton's rule states that an altruistic trait can evolve if the benefit (b) times the coefficient of relatedness (r) is greater than the cost (c) to the donor. This is expressed as:

\[ b \times r > c \]

Here:
- \( b \): The fitness benefit to the recipient.
- \( c \): The fitness cost to the donor due to the altruistic behavior.
- \( r \): The coefficient of relatedness between the donor and the recipient.

This rule indicates that altruism can be favored by natural selection when the relative fitness benefit of the action to the recipient is multiplied by the relatedness between the donor and recipient, exceeds the cost to the donor. The coefficient of relatedness measures the genetic similarity between individuals, which is crucial for determining whether the benefits outweigh the costs from a genetic perspective.

Hamilton's rule states that an altruistic trait can evolve if the benefit (b) times the coefficient of relatedness (r) is greater than the cost (c) to the donor. This is expressed as:

non_conflictual_elements.title: Genetics, Autosomal Recessive -- Development
non_conflictual_elements.text: Mendelian genetics focuses on disorders caused by single genes, thus excluding polygenic or multifactorial traits. Mendelian genetics is based on the experiments of Gregor Mendel, the Austrian monk who studied garden peas. Mendel described three laws. [1] The first law is the Law of Segregation, which states that each gamete contains one allele for a trait, and it combines with the other gamete to give the offspring a pair of alleles for each trait, one from each parent. The second law is the Law of Independent Assortment, which states that alleles for different traits may segregate and combine independently of each other during meiosis and fertilization. The third law is the Law of Dominance, which states that one allele can be dominant to the other, thereby masking the other if both are present. The masked allele, in this case, is known as the recessive allele.

non_conflictual_elements.title: Genetics: Inheritance Patterns -- Introduction
non_conflictual_elements.text: Mendel’s Law of Dominance states that different forms of a gene, called "alleles," can mask the expression of other alleles, resulting in dominant and recessive traits. The Law of Segregation states that allele pairs separate during gametogenesis, ensuring that each gamete carries only 1 allele for a given gene. Finally, the Law of Independent Assortment posits that alleles of different genes segregate independently during gamete formation. However, modern genetics recognizes exceptions to this principle, most notably genetic linkage, in which genes are located in proximity on the same chromosome. [2]

conflictual_element.title: Parametric probe 4
conflictual_element.text:
A. A decrease in partial pressure of carbon dioxide and an increase in concentration of hydrogen ions

Explanation:
Hyperventilation, which is rapid breathing without a corresponding increase in physical activity, leads to a decrease in carbon dioxide levels in the blood. This is because the respiratory rate is increased to expel more CO2. As a result of lower CO2 levels, the pH of the blood becomes more alkaline due to a shift in the balance of acids and bases within the blood (specifically, the bicarbonate buffer system).

Conversely, the higher rate of breathing also causes a decrease in the concentration of hydrogen ions (H+) in the blood, as they are exhaled along with CO2 during hyperventilation. This change in H+ concentration contributes to the overall decrease in blood pH, resulting in an acidic environment.

Therefore, the correct answer is A: A decrease in partial pressure of carbon dioxide and an increase in concentration of hydrogen ions.

non_conflictual_elements.title: Physiology, Carbon Dioxide Transport -- Cellular Level
non_conflictual_elements.text: Carbon dioxide production occurs in cells, mainly during the citric acid cycle in the cytoplasm and mitochondria, respectively. During these successive biochemical reactions, the energy stored in the reduced carbon bonds of fats, sugars, and proteins is gradually liberated in a series of stepwise reactions until the carbon atom is fully oxidized and bound to two oxygen atoms. This final product is carbon dioxide. Like other molecules, carbon dioxide always moves down its concentration gradient from sites of production in the mitochondria and cytosol through the phospholipid membrane and into the extracellular space. However, carbon dioxide diffuses readily, much quicker than oxygen. As the cells produce carbon dioxide, it dissolves into the water of the cytoplasm and continues to build up until it reaches a partial pressure greater than 40 to 45 mmHg. This buildup sets up a concentration gradient down which carbon dioxide can diffuse. From that extracellular space, carbon dioxide molecules freely diffuse through the capillary walls, rapidly equilibrating and increasing the partial pressure of carbon dioxide in the blood from about 40 mmHg on the arterial side of a capillary to 45 to 48 mmHg on the venous side. When a person breathes too fast (hyperventilates), they exhale more carbon dioxide than normal. This leads to a decrease in the partial pressure of carbon dioxide in the blood. Simultaneously, the increased breathing rate can lead to a loss of bicarbonate ions, which results in an increase in the concentration of hydrogen ions in the blood. non_conflictual_elements.title: Parametric probe 2

A. A decrease in partial pressure of carbon dioxide and an increase in concentration of hydrogen ions

Explanation:
Hyperventilation, which is excessive and rapid breathing, results in a decrease in the partial pressure of carbon dioxide (CO2) in the blood. This happens because the lungs remove more CO2 than normal during rapid breathing. The body's pH can be affected due to this change in CO2 levels.

When there is less CO2 in the blood, it leads to a condition called respiratory alkalosis. In this state, the concentration of hydrogen ions (H+) decreases because H+ and CO2 are involved in the bicarbonate buffer system. As CO2 is removed faster than its conversion to H+, the excess CO2 combines with water to form H2CO3, which then dissociates into H+ and HCO3-. This process results in a lower H+ concentration.

Thus, the correct answer is A, as it accurately describes both the decrease in CO2 partial pressure and the corresponding increase in hydrogen ion concentration due to the compensatory mechanisms that occur during respiratory alkalosis.

non_conflictual_elements.title: Genetics, Mutagenesis -- Mechanism -- Endogenous
non_conflictual_elements.text: Errors in DNA repair mechanisms : The DNA damage response (DDR) is a group of mechanisms that sense DNA —errors and promote repair. Errors in repair or mutations affecting the DDR network cause different cancers. There are multiple DNA repair mechanisms, including MMR, base excision repair (BER), nucleotide excision repair (NER), translesion synthesis (TLS), homologous recombination (HR), and nonhomologous end-joining (NHEJ) pathways. A cell is predisposed to DNA damage if these repair mechanisms disappear. For example, xeroderma pigmentosum (a rare autosomal recessive skin disorder that makes a person highly prone to developing skin cancer) is caused by a mutation in the NER pathway, resulting in a build-up of UV-associated damage. The TLS repair system and NHEJ are of interest to endogenous mutagenesis. During DNA replication, high-fidelity polymerases have difficulty passing damaged bases (eg, pyrimidine dimers or crosslinked DNA), which stalls DNA replication. Failure to restart replication can result in double-stranded breaks, chromosomal rearrangements, and cell death. Therefore, it is often beneficial to circumvent these replicative arrests to promote cell survival. One mechanism to accomplish this is the TLS system. TLS involves DNA polymerases with larger active sites that allow them to tolerate and bypass DNA lesions. However, it comes at the expense of lower replication fidelity and high error rates, resulting in a greater likelihood of base substitutions. [10] Otherwise, NHEJ is a repair mechanism for double-stranded DNA breaks. It brings 2 ends of DNA fragments together and doesn't require homologous sequences. Therefore, this can result in deletions and insertions. [11]

conflictual_element.title: Cardiopulmonary Exercise Testing -- Anatomy and Physiology
conflictual_element.text: Many fundamental anatomical concepts are relevant to CPET. Grossly, the cardiopulmonary axis is the organ system of most significant concern. While the heart and lungs can be subdivided into their component organizations (broncho-pulmonary segments and chambers, respectively), it is crucial to appreciate these organs as a closed unit, as each seamlessly regulates the other. One can follow the path of deoxygenated blood returning from the systemic circulation to appreciate the loop. Via the inferior vena cava, this blood is collected in the right atrium and then pumped through the right ventricle into the pulmonary arteries of each lung. These arteries lead the way to smaller capillaries, just as main bronchi lead air to increasingly smaller bronchioles. Gas exchange occurs at the level of the alveoli, during which waste carbon dioxide is exchanged for freshly inspired oxygen. The re-oxygenated blood is then returned to the heart by way of the pulmonary veins. The left atrium and ventricle are then tasked with the collecting and pumping of this blood back through the systemic circulation. The organs themselves receive their blood supplies through the bronchial and coronary vessels, early bifurcations within the systemic circulatory system. By nature of the test, CPET allows for evaluation of the axis’s baseline function as well as compensatory mechanisms during times of physiological stress. The system is a case study on how structure influences function.

One can follow the path of deoxygenated blood returning from the systemic circulation to appreciate the loop. Via the inferior vena cava, this blood is collected in the right atrium and then pumped through the right ventricle into the pulmonary arteries of each lung. These arteries lead the way to smaller capillaries, just as main bronchi lead air to increasingly smaller bronchioles. Gas exchange occurs at the level of the alveoli, during which waste carbon dioxide is exchanged for freshly inspired oxygen. The re-oxygenated blood is then returned to the heart by way of the pulmonary veins. The left atrium and ventricle are then tasked with the collecting and pumping of this blood back through the systemic circulation. The organs themselves receive their blood supplies through the bronchial and coronary vessels, early bifurcations within the systemic circulatory system. By nature of the test, CPET allows for evaluation of the axis’s baseline function as well as compensatory mechanisms during times of physiological stress. The system is a case study on how structure influences function.

Annelids (such as earthworms) and arthropods (such as insects) share the characteristic of having segmented bodies, which allows for flexibility and movement. However, it's important to note that while many annelids do have a closed circulatory system, this is not a universal trait among all annelid species. conflictual_element.title: Anesthesia Machine -- Function -- Types of Anesthesia Circuits
conflictual_element.text: Different types of anesthesia circuits exist. The most commonly used system in the modern-day anesthesia machine is the circle system, but other examples of anesthesia circuits include the Mapleson A, B, C, D (and Bain modification), E, and F (Jackson-Rees) systems. There is a T piece close to the patient for Mapleson D, E, and F systems. [8] The circle system : depending upon the settings of the fresh gas inflow, circle systems can be used as a closed system (fresh gas flow [FGF] = oxygen and anesthetic update), semi-closed system (high FGF, gas exits through the expiratory valve), or semi-open system. They have the benefit of conserving airway moisture and heat while limiting the leakage of anesthetic gases out of the system and into the environment. Disadvantages are discussed below (see "Issues of Concern").

conflictual_element.title: Physiology, Pulmonary Ventilation and Perfusion -- Cellular Level
conflictual_element.text: Gas exchange occurs in the respiratory zone of the lung, where alveoli are present. The respiratory zone of the lung includes respiratory bronchioles, alveolar ducts, alveolar sacs, and alveoli. Thin alveolar septa separate adjacent alveoli. Adjacent alveoli have connections via small openings, called pores of Kohn, that allow for collateral airflow and equalization of pressure between alveoli. The control of opening or closing of alveoli to regulate ventilation occurs at the alveolar duct. The alveolar septum has numerous capillaries and thin walls for gas exchange. In addition to capillary endothelial cells, the alveolar septum contains type I pneumocytes that are very thin and line the alveoli, as well as type II pneumocytes that secrete dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine surfactant to decrease alveolar surface tension. Alveolar macrophages, also known as dust cells, are active in defending against pathogens and irritants. Gas exchange in the alveoli occurs primarily by diffusion. Traveling from the alveoli to capillary blood, gases must pass through alveolar surfactant, alveolar epithelium, basement membrane, and capillary endothelium. conflictual_element.text: The nucleus is the most rigid and largest organelle in the cell, typically occupying its central portion. [23] The name of this organelle comes from its resemblance to a nut within a shell (derived from the Latin " nux " and Greek " karyo ," both meaning nut). conflictual_element.title: Cell_Biology_Alberts
conflictual_element.text: Animals live by eating other organisms. Thus, despite their remarkable diversity, animals as different as worms, mollusks, insects, and vertebrates share anatomical features that are fundamental to this way of life. Epidermal cells form a protective outer layer; gut cells absorb nutrients from ingested food; muscle cells allow movement; and neurons and sensory cells control behavior. These diverse cell types are organized into tissues and organs, forming a sheet of skin covering the exterior, a mouth for feeding, and an internal gut tube to digest food—with muscles, nerves, and other tissues arranged in the space between the skin and the gut tube. Many animals have clearly defined axes—an anteroposterior axis, with mouth and brain anterior and anus posterior; a dorsoventral axis, with back dorsal and belly ventral; and a left-right axis. In this section, we discuss some fundamental mechanisms underlying animal development, beginning with how the basic animal body plan is established.

conflictual_element.title: Histology, Cell -- Introduction
conflictual_element.text: The cell is the basic organizational unit of life. All living organisms consist of cells, which are categorized into 2 types based on the presence or absence of a nucleus. Eukaryotic cells (derived from Greek, with " eu " meaning true and " karyo " referring to the nucleus) possess a well-defined nucleus and are found in humans, animals, and plants (see Image . Animal Cell). In contrast, prokaryotic cells, such as certain bacteria and blue-green algae, lack a distinct nucleus, with nuclear material dispersed within the cytoplasm. Cells with similar structures and functions assemble to form tissue. Tissues are classified into 4 primary types: epithelial, connective, muscular, and nervous. Organs consist of combinations of these tissues. The total number, type, size, and shape of cells collectively determine an organism’s size, structure, and function. [1]

conflictual_element.title: Histology, Cell -- Introduction
conflictual_element.text: The cell is the basic organizational unit of life. All living organisms consist of cells, which are categorized into 2 types based on the presence or absence of a nucleus. Eukaryotic cells (derived from Greek, with " eu " meaning true and " karyo " referring to the nucleus) possess a well-defined nucleus and are found in humans, animals, and plants (see Image . Animal Cell). In contrast, prokaryotic cells, such as certain bacteria and blue-green algae, lack a distinct nucleus, with nuclear material dispersed within the cytoplasm. Cells with similar structures and functions assemble to form tissue. Tissues are classified into 4 primary types: epithelial, connective, muscular, and nervous. Organs consist of combinations of these tissues. The total number, type, size, and shape of cells collectively determine an organism’s size, structure, and function. [1]

conflictual_element.title: Partial Pressure of Oxygen -- Other Issues
conflictual_element.text: In conclusion, oxygen is essential to the successful adaptation and proliferation of virtually all life. The 2 identical oxygen molecules chemically connected by a dynamic double bond serve as the fuel source for aerobic metabolism within all mammals. This diatomic structure provides oxygen with the inherent stability necessary for cellular and membrane transport within the mitochondrial apparatus. Although perhaps not the most numerically significant gas in Earth's atmosphere, oxygen surely remains the most important for supporting life. The delicate interplay between the 21% oxygen gas in Earth's atmosphere, the 78% nitrogen, and trace amounts of carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) is essential for sustaining all life dependent on aerobic metabolism. Only bacteria capable of anaerobic metabolism, along with viruses, can exist in the absence of the life-giving oxygen molecule. At sea level, atmospheric pressure remains constant at 760 mmHg. The composition of this pressure includes the partial pressures of nitrogen at 593 mmHg, oxygen at 160 mmHg, and a much smaller contribution from water vapor. Although nitrogen (N 2 ) is considered physiologically inert, it too contributes substantially to atmospheric and alveolar stability (see I mages Components of Air and Partial Pressure at STPD (1 atm, 0 °c, 0% Humidity) and Partial Pressures of Respiratory Gases in Air Samples and Blood).

conflictual_element.text: K. plaskitt.) Figure 14–38 A mitochondrion and chloroplast compared. Chloroplasts are generally larger than mitochondria. In addition to an outer and inner envelope membrane, they contain the thylakoid membrane with its internal thylakoid space. the chloroplast thylakoid membrane, which is the site of solar energy conversion in plants and algae, corresponds to the mitochondrial cristae, which are the sites of energy conversion by cellular respiration. Unlike the crista membrane, which is continuous with the inner mitochondrial membrane at cristae junctions, the thylakoid membrane is not connected to the inner chloroplast membrane at any point.

conflictual_element.title: Cell_Biology_Alberts
conflictual_element.text: New mitochondria and chloroplasts are produced by the growth of preexisting organelles, followed by fission (discussed in Chapter 14). The growth depends mainly on the import of proteins from the cytosol. The imported proteins must be transported across a number of membranes in succession and end up in the appropriate place. The process of protein movement across membranes is called protein translocation. This section explains how it occurs. Figure 12–19 The subcompartments of mitochondria and chloroplasts. in contrast to the cristae of mitochondria (a), the thylakoids of chloroplasts (B) are not connected to the inner membrane and therefore form a sealed compartment with a separate internal space.

non_conflictual_elements.text: The mitochondrion consists of inner and outer membranes, both of which are composed of phospholipid bilayers and integral membrane proteins involved in enzymatic action and molecular transport.
